rock_grade: Class 3 (brief exposed Class 3-4 moves at the summit block)
face: North/notch side of the summit block
overview: Bulls Tooth is a striking granite summit on the arcuate ridge rimming Chain and Doelle Lakes in the Chiwaukum Mountains, about 5.5 miles southeast of Stevens Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest). It's one of the longest approaches out of Stevens Pass -- roughly 10 miles one-way via the PCT, Icicle Creek Trail, and the steep, unswitchbacked Chain Lakes Trail (#1569) -- rewarding backpackers with a quiet basin and a short, airy Class 3 scramble to a broad summit
beta: Bulls Tooth has no maintained summit trail. Parties reach the base via the Chain Lakes basin — a scenic, blueberry-covered alpine bench in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness — then climb through steep heather, mossy slabs, brush, and short cliff bands to boulder fields below the summit block, finishing on a short, exposed Class 3 pitch of looser, sandier rock near the top. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no cairned or established line.
breakdown: Chain Lakes to boulder fields: Class 2-3

first_pass.evidence: One party reports Class 2 scrambling on the north side of the summit block; easiest route listed simply as a scramble

fa: Don Williamson, Bill Bucher, and Tom Oas, 1971
overview: A rarely repeated technical new route established in 1971 up Burnt Boot Peak's north ridge: three leads of low-to-mid class 5 granite culminating on a knife-edge crest, followed by three easier leads of class 3-4 scrambling to the summit.
beta: Burnt Boot Peak (P 6480) sits across the Middle Fork of the Snoqualmie River, about two miles southeast of Big Snow Mountain. From the base of the steepest part of the north ridge, three leads of fifth class on granite, the last along a very sharp crest, reach easier ground; three more leads of class 3 and 4 gain the summit. The peak's first ascent, by a 1963 survey party, came by an easier scramble line. No repeat ascents of the ridge are recorded, so expect little to no modern traffic.

first_pass.evidence: No online source found; record describes three leads of low-to-mid class 5 granite then Class 3-4
first_pass.note: No number exists anywhere; 5.0 per the low-5th rule, may be harder.

overview: An alternate line up Cardinal Peak's north side, approached via Saska Basin/Pass rather than the direct basin camp used for the Southeast Slopes route; most often climbed as part of multi-peak traverses of the Chelan Mountains (Saska, Emerald, Pinnacle, Cardinal).
beta: Climbs a couloir on the northwest side to gain the north ridge, then follows the ridge toward the summit. Multiple parties report the north ridge holding snow and verglas well into the season, which has forced several groups to abandon the ridge partway and traverse instead onto the peak's east/southeast slopes (see Southeast Slopes) to finish the climb.

first_pass.evidence: Broad scree/talus NW couloir gains the north ridge; the true (south) summit block needs ~20 ft of 4th class/low 5th
first_pass.note: Ridge itself is scrambling; 5.0 applies only if the south-summit block is climbed.

overview: An alternate, US-side non-technical line up Castle Peak from Castle Creek Basin, climbing a wide south-facing gully to a northeast gully and a roughly 7,400-ft notch high on the mountain, then a short scramble to the summit.
beta: Distinct from the East Ridge Couloir/Southeast Ridge line, this route stays on the peak's south side. From a camp near 5,500 ft in Castle Creek Basin, ascend the wide gully on the south side to about 6,800 ft, then enter the northeast gully aiming for a notch around 7,400 ft. The final section crosses granite slabs, boulders and snow patches with a short scramble to the true summit.

first_pass.evidence: NE gully to the 7,400-ft notch, then slabs and boulders to the south face of the summit block: class 3+ with route finding; class 4 can be unavoidable once snow has melted

face: North Ridge (Chair) to the Bryant col/ridge crest
overview: An alpine ridge linkup that starts on Chair Peak's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant Peak, with parties often extending the traverse further to The Tooth or even Denny Mountain for a longer high-route day.
beta: Pitch-by-pitch beta for this line is not available. It begins on Chair's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant on 4th-class to low-5th-class rock, with one short, steep mandatory rappel (~50 ft) getting off Bryant — the same rappel found on the closely related 'Tooth - Chair Traverse,' which covers the Bryant-to-Chair portion of this ridge system.

first_pass.evidence: No graded write-up of the Chair-Bryant traverse found; the same ridge done as the Tooth-Chair Traverse is 5.4 Grade III on MP (4th/low 5th rock, one short rappel off Bryant).
first_pass.note: Nothing supports the record's 5.7; 5.4 is borrowed from the overlapping Tooth-Chair traverse.

overview: Cinderella Peak (roughly 6,400-6,500 ft) is a minor summit on the south side of the Green Creek cirque in the Twin Sisters Range, immediately west of Mount Baker and within/adjacent to the Mount Baker Wilderness (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest). The Twin Sisters massif is the largest exposed body of dunite/olivine rock in the Western Hemisphere, giving Cinderella and its neighbors (Little Sister, South Twin, Skookum, Jaws' Tooth) their signature reddish, ultra-grippy slabs. The standard ro
beta: A short but rugged Twin Sisters Range outing combining glacier travel with class 3-4 scrambling on famously high-friction olivine rock. Parties reach the peak via the Green Creek cirque in one long day or with a night in the basin, and climb it either as a stand-alone objective or as part of the longer Green Creek Circuit traverse linking South Sister, Skookum, Little Sister, and Cinderella.

first_pass.evidence: West ridge is mostly hiking, then 'fun scrambling' to the true summit (no class given); the record's 4th class finish could not be confirmed or refuted.

rock_grade: 5.8+ (or 5.2 with A1 aid at the crux headwall, per a 2016 repeat)
face: Northwest Couloir - North Ridge - West Face - South Ridge (per a detailed 2016 account); a 1963 account describes it as a diagonal gully and chimney system to the first notch north of the summit, then a traverse of the ridge and ledges to the summit
fa: Ardussi, Magnusson, Mech, Swanson (The Mountaineers) — July 31, 1963
overview: Crooked Thumb Peak (8,129 ft) sits on the Northern Pickets crest exactly 0.5 mi south of Mount Challenger and 0.5 mi north of Phantom Peak, in North Cascades National Park's Whatcom County backcountry. The true summit is a striking, narrow 'fin' of white gneiss/granite only about 5 ft high — Fred and Helmy Beckey made the first ascent in 1940, and remarkably no one is recorded returning to sign the register until Phil Sharpe, Vic Josendal, and Warren Spickard's second ascent 18 years later in 19
beta: This classic Beckey-era first ascent combines a roughly 46-50 mile round-trip backpacking approach with technical alpine climbing. The route is accessed via the Hannegan Trailhead system, passing through the Chilliwack River drainage to Whatcom Pass, then crossing Whatcom Glacier and the heavily crevassed Crooked Thumb Glacier to reach the moraine basecamp. The summit push ascends the obvious northwest couloir with simul-climbing on 40-45 degree snow using snow flukes for protection, transitioni
breakdown: Approach: Hannegan TH to Copper Creek Camp: Class 2, moderate backpack terrain
Approach: Copper Creek to Whatcom Pass: Class 2-3 backpack
Approach: Whatcom Pass to Crooked Thumb Glacier Moraine: Class 2-3, glacier travel
Northwest Couloir: 45-degree snow slopes, Class 4-5 rock exit
North Ridge to Summit: Class 4, exposed

first_pass.evidence: 2016 report: summit headwall crack is 5.8+ free or 5.2/A1; their party aided it.
first_pass.note: Only one route-specific source. The aid option is A1.

face: Northeast Face — the 5,250-ft wall above Stetattle Creek
fa: Dallas Kloke and Bryce Simon, July 12, 1976. First winter ascent (to the summit ridge): Stuart Taylor and Ade Miller, March 13, 2005
overview: The Northeast Face Couloir climbs Davis Peak's huge northeast wall above Stetattle Creek, one of the biggest faces in the North Cascades: a compact lower rock band, a traverse left across a large snowfield, belayed crux pitches over iced slabs and a steep chockstone, then a long, exposed upper couloir to the cornices where it meets the summit ridge near 6,700 ft. It goes in summer as a rock-and-snow route and has been climbed in winter; the descent is the long south side.
beta: From a bivouac at about 4,000 ft at the foot of the glacier, climb the glacier to the bergschrund and simul-climb the compact lower rock band (mid-fifth class in summer, hard to protect) to the right side of the large snowfield. Traverse left across the snowfield to the couloir, belay the crux pitches over iced slabs and a steep chockstone, and continue up the long, exposed upper couloir to the cornices where it meets the summit ridge at about 6,700 ft. The summit is a short way along the ridge.

first_pass.evidence: Sources confirm the North Face Couloir in the NE face (Kloke/Simon 1972) but give no online grade; record's 5.6 kept.
first_pass.note: Burdo's 1988 AAJ report says his IV 5.10 central chimney was 'probably the melted-out version of the 1974 Kloke-Simon route', so this couloir and wa_davis_peak_nc_north_face_burdo_cairns may share a line.

overview: Hidden Couloir is the entry gully of Dragontail's north-face ice and mixed complex — it is the first of the three couloirs linked by the popular Triple Couloirs route. It starts around 6,400 ft directly above the south end of Colchuck Lake and, true to its name, is hidden from view from the lake itself. The couloir climbs roughly 800 vertical feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice before joining broader terrain higher on the face; some parties climb just this lower section as a shorter half-day objec
beta: Named for being out of view from Colchuck Lake, this couloir starts at roughly 6,400 ft directly above the lake's south end and trends south for about 800 vertical feet at roughly 45°, typically holding good neve snow into mid-summer. Climbed alone, most parties top out at the steep rock band (the top of the Runnels crux) rather than continuing into the second and third couloirs.

first_pass.evidence: Hidden Couloir is the first couloir of Triple Couloirs: ~800 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice; no separate ice grade found (Triple Couloirs overall WI3 M3, its crux is above this couloir).
first_pass.note: Mapped steep snow (40-50 deg, front-pointing) to Class 3; if the couloir is icy it may merit AI2 as the record says.

face: West side, approached via the col shared with West McMillan Spire
overview: East McMillan Spire (7,992 ft) is the lower, eastern summit of the McMillan Spires, twin granite towers just 0.14 mile apart in the Southern Pickets, North Cascades National Park. It sits directly across a low-fifth-class connecting ridge from its taller twin, West McMillan Spire (8,004 ft), and the two are almost always climbed together from a shared high camp in Terror Basin. Fred and Helmy Beckey made pioneering first ascents throughout the McMillan group during their 1940 forays into the Pic
beta: Most parties climb East McMillan Spire as an add-on to West McMillan Spire via the shared Terror Basin/West Ridge approach, then traverse east along the connecting ridge crest (roughly 5.6) to tag the lower, eastern summit.

first_pass.evidence: Trip report: steep snow gully to the East-West col, some 4th class to reach the saddle, then 'easy 3rd class terrain to East McMillan's summit'. The 5.6-5.7 Beckey line cited online is the West McMillan side of the col.
first_pass.note: MP says there is no non-technical route; a short low-5th move may be met depending on line. Headline 'Grade III, 5.6' also clashes with commitment II.
